blocks.text: Every aluminium window frame, copper tube and drawn guitar string started as a thick billet or rod forced through a die smaller than itself. The die does the shaping and the press or draw bench only has to supply enough force to flow the metal through it, which is a force you can estimate from the area ratio alone.

blocks.markdown: In **extrusion** a billet of cross-sectional area $A_0$ is pushed by a ram through a die opening of area $A_f$, producing a long product of constant section. In **drawing** a rod or wire is pulled through a die by a force applied at the exit. In both, the metal is squeezed to a smaller area; the difference is that extrusion pushes (the metal is in compression, so large reductions are possible) while drawing pulls (the exit wire is in tension and must stay strong enough to carry the draw force).

blocks.title: Extrusion ratio and reduction
blocks.text: The extrusion ratio is $R_x=A_0/A_f$. The reduction in area is $r=(A_0-A_f)/A_0=1-1/R_x$. The true strain in an ideal reduction is $\varepsilon=\ln(A_0/A_f)=\ln R_x$.

blocks.caption: Ideal (frictionless, perfectly plastic) extrusion pressure and ram force. $Y_f$ is the average flow stress in MPa; real pressure is higher because of container friction and redundant work

blocks.title: Extrusion pressure and ram force
blocks.prompt: A hot aluminium billet of diameter 100 mm is extruded to a round rod of diameter 25 mm. Take $Y_f=150$ MPa as a typical hot flow stress. Find the extrusion ratio, ideal pressure and ram force.

steps.text: Ram force on the billet area $A_0=7854$ mm$^2$.

blocks.answer: R_x = 16, ideal pressure is about 416 MPa and the ram force is at least 3.27 MN (real force is higher because of friction).

blocks.markdown: In practice, extrusion pressure is higher than the ideal value because friction at the die and, in direct extrusion, along the container wall adds work. Two arrangements are used. In **forward (direct) extrusion** the ram and the product move in the same direction, so the billet slides along the container wall and friction force builds up in proportion to the remaining billet length. In **backward (indirect) extrusion** the die is carried on a hollow ram that moves into the billet; the billet does not move relative to the container wall, so the container friction is absent.

rows: Cans and cups (impact extrusion), tubes closed at one end
Butt left in the container, high force
blocks.caption: Forward and backward extrusion compared

blocks.markdown: **Drawing** applies the same ideas to wire, rod and tube. A rod of initial area $A_0$ is pulled through a die to area $A_f$. For an ideal pass with no friction and no redundant work, the draw stress at the exit equals the mean flow stress times the true strain. The draw force is that stress times the exit area, because the exit wire carries the whole pull. For the wire not to neck or fracture, the draw stress must stay below the exit wire's flow stress, which caps the reduction per pass.

blocks.caption: Ideal draw stress, force and reduction in area for round wire ($\bar Y$ is the mean flow stress, $d$ diameter)

blocks.title: One pass of wire drawing
blocks.prompt: Copper-like wire of diameter 5.0 mm is drawn to 4.2 mm in one pass. Take a mean flow stress $\bar Y=300$ MPa (typical for work-hardened copper). Find the reduction, ideal draw stress and draw force.
blocks.answer: The reduction is about 29.4 percent, the ideal draw stress 105 MPa and the draw force about 1.45 kN.

blocks.title: Why drawing takes small steps
blocks.text: In the ideal limit the draw stress equals $\bar Y$ when $\ln(A_0/A_f)=1$, i.e. a reduction of $1-e^{-1}=63$ percent. Friction and redundant work make the real limit lower, so production wire drawing usually takes reductions of about 20 to 30 percent per pass and uses many dies in a row. Extrusion, being a compressive process, can take reductions of 90 percent or more in one pass.

blocks.title: Ideal formulas are lower bounds
blocks.text: The $\ln R_x$ pressure ignores container friction, die friction and redundant deformation, so a real press needs more force, sometimes 30 to 100 percent more (a typical range, not a rule). Size equipment with a margin and check against measured data.

points: Extrusion ratio $R_x=A_0/A_f$ gives the ideal pressure $p=Y_f\ln R_x$ and ram force $F=pA_0$.
Wire drawing reduction is $r=1-(d_f/d_0)^2$, with ideal draw stress $\sigma_d=\bar Y\ln(A_0/A_f)$ and force $F_d=\sigma_dA_f$.
Drawing is limited by the strength of the exit wire, so reductions are small; extrusion is compressive and allows large reductions.
Forward extrusion suits long sections but has container friction; backward extrusion avoids it and is used for cups and cans.

questions.stem: A billet of cross-sectional area $A_0$ is extruded through a die of area $A_f$. How is the extrusion ratio defined?

distractorRationale.a: This is the inverse; it is the area ratio that gives values above 1 for reduction.
distractorRationale.c: This is the reduction in area $r$, not the extrusion ratio.
distractorRationale.d: This is a negative strain-like quantity; the ideal strain uses $\ln(A_0/A_f)$.

questions.explanation: The extrusion ratio is the original over final area, always greater than one. The reduction in area $1-1/R_x$ and the strain $\ln R_x$ are derived from it.

questions.stem: A hot aluminium billet of cross-section 3000 mm$^2$ is extruded through a die of area 250 mm$^2$. Take a mean flow stress of 120 MPa. Calculate the ideal ram force in kN using $p=Y_f\ln R_x$ and $F=pA_0$.
questions.explanation: The extrusion ratio is $R_x=3000/250=12$, so $p=120\ln12=120(2.485)=298.2$ MPa. The ram force is $F=298.2\times3000=894566$ N, about 895 kN, which is the minimum because friction is ignored.

questions.stem: For ideal extrusion with $p=Y_f\ln R_x$, what happens to the ideal pressure if the extrusion ratio is doubled?

distractorRationale.a: Pressure depends on the logarithm of $R_x$, not on $R_x$ itself, so doubling $R_x$ does not double the pressure.
distractorRationale.b: The pressure clearly increases with the strain imposed on the material.
distractorRationale.c: A larger reduction requires more, not less, work per unit volume.

questions.explanation: Since $\ln(2R_x)=\ln R_x+\ln2$, the pressure increases by an additive $Y_f\ln2\approx0.69Y_f$. Because of the logarithm, large extrusion ratios are reached with moderate extra pressure.

questions.stem: A steel wire of diameter 3.0 mm is drawn through a die to a diameter of 2.4 mm. Calculate the reduction in area as a percentage.
questions.explanation: The areas scale with the square of diameter, so $r=1-(2.4/3.0)^2=1-0.64=0.36$. The reduction in area is 36 percent.

questions.stem: A wire of diameter 6.0 mm is drawn to 5.0 mm in a single ideal pass with mean flow stress 200 MPa. Calculate the draw force in N using $\sigma_d=\bar Y\ln(A_0/A_f)$ and $F_d=\sigma_dA_f$.
In an ideal wire-drawing pass (no friction, no redundant work, perfectly plastic wire) what is the maximum reduction in area before the draw stress reaches the flow stress of the exit wire?

distractorRationale.b: 37 percent is the area ratio $A_f/A_0=e^{-1}$, not the reduction.
distractorRationale.d: 100 percent would mean zero exit area, which gives infinite strain.

questions.explanation: The draw stress equals $\bar Y\ln(A_0/A_f)$ and reaches $\bar Y$ when $\ln(A_0/A_f)=1$, i.e. $A_f/A_0=e^{-1}=0.368$. The reduction is then $1-0.368=63$ percent, and real friction lowers this limit.

questions.stem: A manufacturer wants to make closed-end aluminium aerosol cans by a single stroke of a punch into a slug. Which extrusion arrangement is the natural choice?

options.text: Forward (direct) extrusion through a long die

distractorRationale.a: Forward extrusion pushes metal through a die to make an open long section, not a closed cup.
distractorRationale.b: Drawing pulls a rod through a die; it does not form a cup shape.
distractorRationale.d: Rolling produces flat sheet or sections, not cans.

questions.explanation: In backward extrusion the metal flows back along the punch, forming a cup with a closed end; the punch is the ram and the wall is formed in the gap. It is used for cans, tubes with one closed end and similar cup-like parts.

questions.stem: Why does forward (direct) extrusion need a higher ram force than backward (indirect) extrusion of the same billet and die?

options.text: The die angle is always steeper
The flow stress is higher in forward extrusion
Backward extrusion avoids all deformation work
The billet slides along the container wall, adding friction

questions.correctOptionText: The billet slides along the container wall, adding friction

distractorRationale.a: Die geometry is chosen independently; it is not the systematic difference.
distractorRationale.b: Flow stress is a material and temperature property, not set by the direction of the ram.
distractorRationale.c: Both processes need the same ideal deformation work; only the friction term differs.

questions.explanation: In direct extrusion the billet moves relative to the stationary container, so friction along the wall adds to the force until the billet is almost used up. Indirect extrusion moves the die with the billet, so that friction is absent, though ram strength limits the product size.

questions.stem: A company needs (a) 6 m lengths of an aluminium window-frame profile and (b) thousands of aluminium toothpaste-tube-like closed-end tubes. Recommend forward or backward extrusion for each and justify your choice in terms of product shape, force and friction.
markingGuide: (a) Forward extrusion for long open sections with large cross-section
Billet slides in the container so friction is high but ram can be strong and billet length large
(b) Backward (impact) extrusion for closed-end tubes: metal flows back around the punch
No relative movement between billet and container, so lower friction and force
Notes drawbacks: butt left behind in (a); size limited by hollow ram in indirect extrusion
questions.explanation: Long open profiles are made by forward extrusion because the ram pushes the billet through a stationary die, even though container friction raises the force. Closed-end tubes are made by backward extrusion, where the punch forms the cavity and the metal flows back.

questions.stem: Explain why wire drawing is done in many small reductions (typically a fraction of the ideal 63 percent limit) whereas an extruder can reduce a billet by 95 percent in one pass. Refer to the stresses acting on the product.
markingGuide: Drawing pulls the wire through the die, so the exit wire is in tension
The draw stress must be less than the flow stress (strength) of the exit wire or it necks and fractures
Ideal limit $\ln(A_0/A_f)=1$ gives 63 percent; friction and redundant work lower the real limit
Extrusion pushes the billet through the die so the work is in compression and the product does not carry the load
Therefore large extrusion ratios are possible; drawing needs multiple dies and intermediate anneals for work hardening
questions.explanation: In drawing the pulling force is carried by the thinned wire, which limits the draw stress to its own strength and caps the reduction per pass. In extrusion the force is applied by a ram in compression, so no weak exit section limits the reduction.
